item.title: The Hidden Risk in MCP Connections
item.description: Thanks, Traceforce, for sponsoring this article.
item.dc:creator: Ken Huang
item.content:encoded:
Thanks, Traceforce, for sponsoring this article.

AI is learning to use the tools around it. That is the promise of the Model Context Protocol, and it is also the security shift many teams are underestimating.

For the last two years, most enterprise AI conversations have centered on model behavior: hallucination, prompt injection, data leakage, evaluation, and policy. Those risks still matter. But the practical risk is changing as assistants move from answering questions to taking actions. When an assistant can query a data warehouse, open a browser, read a file, create a ticket, send a message, update a document, or run a build, the security question is no longer only “what did the model say?” It becomes “what did the system allow the model-connected workflow to do?”

MCP sits directly inside that question.

This is also where a registry-plus-scanner pattern matters: treat MCP not as a one-off connector choice, but as an inventory and governance surface with a review and update loop. Traceforce’s public Atlas registry at

https://atlas.traceforce.co/

gives teams a reference point for known MCP servers and security ratings, while its open-source MCP X-Ray scanner helps teams inspect the MCP servers already present in local and enterprise environments.

MCP is not a model. It is not an agent framework. It is a connection layer: a standard way for AI hosts, such as chat applications, IDEs, and agent runtimes, to connect to external tools, data sources, and services. The official MCP specification describes a host, an MCP client inside that host, and MCP servers that expose resources, prompts, and tools. Anthropic introduced MCP in November 2024 as an open standard for connecting AI assistants to systems where data lives, replacing one-off integrations with a common protocol. The current public protocol version, 2025-11-25 as of July 2026, frames MCP as a way to share context, expose capabilities, and build composable workflows.

That is powerful. It is also exactly why MCP deserves a security review that looks different from a normal API review.

An API integration usually lives behind application code. Developers decide which endpoint to call, what parameters are allowed, how credentials are stored, where logs go, and which user action triggered the request. MCP makes integrations easier to add, easier to discover, and easier for AI tools to invoke. The upside is speed. The downside is that every new MCP connection creates a fresh trust boundary between a probabilistic reasoning system, executable tool code, enterprise data, and downstream APIs.

If a connection can only read a public weather API, the boundary may be low risk. If it can read Slack, browse internal Drive folders, query Snowflake, write GitHub issues, run shell commands, update CRM records, or access regulated data, the boundary becomes a control point. It needs identity, permission, policy, runtime containment, and traceability. Without those, MCP can turn a local productivity feature into an ungoverned action path.

Figure 1 illustrates the architectural reason this happens. MCP simplifies the connection pattern, but it also creates a repeatable path from AI intent to external action.

The risk is not that MCP is inherently unsafe. The risk is that MCP makes capability feel like configuration. A user or team adds a server, the host sees a list of tools, the model gets descriptions of those tools, and suddenly the assistant has a path into places it could not reach before. That path may be authorized in the narrow sense that a token exists. It may still be poorly governed in the security sense: too much privilege, too little review, unclear ownership, weak logs, and no practical way to reconstruct what happened during an incident.

This is the hidden risk in MCP connections: they look like integrations, but they behave like delegated agency.

MCP is a connection layer, not a permission model

The simplest way to understand MCP is to separate the protocol from the policy around it.

The protocol standardizes how AI applications talk to external systems. Servers can offer resources, which are data and context; prompts, which are templated workflows; and tools, which are functions the AI system can execute. Clients can also expose capabilities such as roots, sampling, and elicitation, depending on implementation. The base protocol uses JSON-RPC messages, supports capability negotiation, and lets hosts connect to many servers through a common pattern.

That standardization solves a real engineering problem. Before MCP, each AI application and each business system needed a custom integration. If there are N AI applications and M tools, the integration surface becomes N times M. MCP reduces that by giving tool builders one protocol to expose capabilities and host builders one protocol to consume them.

Security teams should appreciate that benefit. Standardization can make controls easier. A common protocol can support common gateways, registries, policy checks, observability, and review processes. The mistake is assuming the protocol itself supplies all those controls by default.

The MCP specification includes important security principles: explicit user consent, user control over shared data and actions, data privacy, tool safety, and caution around LLM sampling. It also says that tools can represent arbitrary code execution and should be treated carefully. The official security best practices document goes further, covering confused deputy risks, token passthrough, SSRF, session hijacking, local server compromise, stdio transport risks, and scope minimization.

But a protocol specification is not an enterprise governance program. It cannot know whether a server should access engineering repositories but not payroll data. It cannot decide whether a “send email” tool is acceptable for an intern’s agent but not for a production support bot. It cannot guarantee that a community MCP server is maintained, sandboxed, patched, or logging the right fields. It cannot infer whether a broad OAuth scope was granted because the workflow needed it or because the consent prompt was easier to implement.

That is why the security posture of MCP depends on the environment around each connection. The core question is not “does this server speak MCP?” The question is “what does this connection allow, on whose behalf, under which policy, with which evidence trail?”

Every connection creates a new trust boundary

Security teams already know trust boundaries from application design. A browser boundary. A service boundary. A database boundary. A tenant boundary. A network boundary. MCP adds a boundary that is less familiar because it combines four moving parts:

First, there is a user or workflow expressing intent in natural language. The prompt may be precise, vague, incomplete, or adversarially influenced by content the model has read.

Second, there is an AI host deciding what to do. It may summarize, reason, plan, select tools, call tools, inspect outputs, and continue the task.

Third, there is an MCP server exposing capabilities. That server may be local or remote, official or community-maintained, read-only or action-capable, narrow or broad, trusted or merely installed.

Fourth, there is a downstream system that treats a request as an API call, file access, browser operation, or database query.

The trust boundary appears wherever assumptions change. User intent is not the same as model interpretation. Model interpretation is not the same as policy approval. MCP tool metadata is not the same as trusted code. A token is not the same as least privilege. A downstream API log is not the same as an agent audit trail.

Figure 2 shows the practical version of this: trust should be checked at each handoff, not allowed to flow automatically through the whole chain.

The NSA’s May 2026 security design guidance for MCP makes this point directly: organizations should define trust boundaries between agents, plugins, models, and users, and should treat them as separate trust zones with different assumptions and controls. The guidance also warns that dynamic tool discovery should be paired with origin verification or authorization checks, and recommends aligning tools and models with data classification zones.

That advice matters because MCP connections often arrive through operational convenience. A developer wants the AI assistant to read the repository. A sales team wants it to query CRM. A support team wants it to search tickets and draft responses. A data team wants it to inspect warehouse schemas. The natural question becomes “can we connect this?” The security question should be “where is the boundary, and what changes when this connection is added?”

A connection to GitHub may create a boundary between an AI host and source code. A connection to a filesystem may create a boundary between a chat prompt and local secrets. A connection to Slack may create a boundary between generated reasoning and private conversation history. A connection to a database may create a boundary between natural-language exploration and sensitive records. A connection to a browser automation tool may create a boundary between the assistant and any web app the user is logged into.

None of those boundaries is automatically wrong. Each simply needs a design. The risk appears when teams add connections faster than they add boundary controls.

The first failure mode: overbroad permissions

The easiest MCP security mistake is giving a connection more authority than the workflow actually needs.

Overbroad permissions are familiar in cloud security: wildcard IAM policies, long-lived access keys, service accounts with too many roles, broad SaaS OAuth grants, and shared admin tokens. MCP gives that old problem a new route. A tool may be added for a narrow job, but the token or local runtime may allow much more than the job requires.

The official MCP security best practices warn that broad scopes increase compromise impact, obscure audit trails, and allow privilege chaining. The document recommends progressive least privilege: start with minimal baseline scopes, elevate only when a privileged operation is attempted, and log elevation events with correlation IDs. It also calls out common mistakes such as wildcard scopes, omnibus “full access” grants, bundling unrelated privileges, and treating claimed token scopes as sufficient without server-side authorization logic.

That last point is important. A token is not a policy engine. If a server accepts a token and then exposes every tool to the client, the user-facing permission model may be much broader than the consent moment implied.

There are several versions of this problem.

One version is server-level access without tool-level access. A user is approved to connect to a project-management MCP server because they need to read tickets. But the server also exposes tools to close tickets, edit priorities, change assignees, delete records, or administer projects. If the authorization decision happens only at the server level, the connection is effectively all-or-nothing.

Another version is broad SaaS scopes. A workflow needs to read one folder, one repository, or one issue tracker project, but the OAuth grant covers all files, all repositories, or all projects the user can access. If the agent, prompt, or server is compromised, the blast radius becomes the full scope of the token, not the narrow task the user had in mind.

A third version is local authority. Local MCP servers can inherit access from the operating system account or local environment. A filesystem server may be configured to a project root, but another tool may expose shell execution. A browser tool may reach whatever the browser session can reach. A database tool may use an environment variable with powerful credentials. These local conveniences make prototypes fast. They also make privilege boundaries easy to blur.

Figure 3 captures the blast radius difference between a narrow grant and a broad grant. The user asked for the same task in both lanes. The permission shape changes the consequence of misuse.

Security teams should assume that every MCP server exposes a capability catalog, not a single feature. The catalog needs classification. Which tools are read-only? Which write? Which are destructive? Which administer identity, policy, billing, secrets, or infrastructure? Which can execute code? Which can move data outside the organization?

The permission model should follow that classification. Read-only discovery should not require write scopes. Write tools should require stronger consent and policy checks. Destructive or admin tools should require step-up approval, break-glass logging, or may not belong in general-purpose assistants at all. Sensitive tools should be scoped by data class, tenant, project, and environment.

The test is simple: if the user asked the assistant to do one task and the token would allow ten unrelated tasks, the connection is over-privileged.

The second failure mode: weak auditing

If overbroad permissions increase blast radius, weak auditing removes the map.

MCP actions can cross several systems. A user prompt may lead to an agent decision, then an MCP tool call, then a downstream API request, then a database row change, then a summarized result. A normal SaaS audit log may record the API request, but it may not know the agent’s prompt, tool selection, approval state, or reasoning path. The AI host may know that a tool was called, but not how the downstream service interpreted the token. The MCP server may log the method name but not the user, trace ID, policy decision, sanitized parameters, or result.

That fragmentation is dangerous. In an incident, the questions are concrete:

  • Which user or agent principal initiated the action?

  • Which host and MCP client made the request?

  • Which server, version, and tool were invoked?

  • What scopes and policies allowed it?

  • What input parameters were sent?

  • What downstream resource was read or changed?

  • What output came back?

  • Was any sensitive data included in the model context?

  • Was the action approved, denied, retried, escalated, or hidden inside a larger workflow?

If the organization cannot answer those questions, it does not have an audit trail. It has scattered logs.

CoSAI’s 2026 MCP security report lists insufficient logging, monitoring, and auditability as a core threat category. The report warns that without robust logging of MCP connections, tool invocations, authorization decisions, and data access patterns, organizations face compliance blind spots and weak forensics. Red Hat’s April 2026 guidance makes the operational version of the same point: detailed audit trails, structured logging, metrics, sandboxing, rate limits, and input sanitization turn an MCP environment from a black box into a traceable system.

Figure 4 shows the minimum shape. The log should not merely say that “the agent did something.” It should connect the prompt, principal, tool call, policy decision, downstream action, and result.

Good MCP auditing should be structured, centralized, and correlated.

Structured means every event has fields, not just text. At minimum: timestamp, trace ID, user identity, agent identity if distinct, host application, MCP client, MCP server, server version, tool name, action category, requested scopes, granted scopes, policy decision, sanitized parameters, data classification, downstream target, status, error, output size, and risk flags.

Centralized means events flow to a system the security team controls, such as a SIEM or logging pipeline. Logs that remain only on a developer laptop, inside a local tool, or in a vendor console with limited retention will not support incident response.

Correlated means the same trace ID follows the action chain. A security analyst should be able to start with a suspicious database write and work backward to the MCP tool, agent workflow, user prompt, approval moment, and source host. They should also be able to start with a prompt and work forward to every downstream system touched.

This is not just compliance hygiene. It is how teams distinguish a benign assistant action from data exfiltration, prompt injection, credential misuse, or an overly autonomous workflow. When AI systems act through tools, the ability to trace action becomes a primary safety control.

The third failure mode: trusting tool metadata as if it were code review

MCP tools are presented to models through descriptions, schemas, names, and arguments. That metadata is not harmless documentation. It becomes part of the model’s decision environment.

Security researchers have already shown why this matters. Invariant Labs described tool poisoning attacks in which malicious instructions are embedded in MCP tool descriptions. The user may see a simple, harmless summary of the tool, while the model sees hidden instructions that influence behavior, including attempts to read sensitive files or pass secrets through tool parameters. Unit 42 has also analyzed risks around MCP sampling, where a server can request completions from the client’s LLM. Their research highlights resource theft, conversation hijacking, and covert tool invocation as possible attack paths when malicious servers are connected and safeguards are weak.

These attacks are not identical, but they share a pattern: the model receives instructions or context from a source the user did not fully inspect, then uses tools in ways the user may not expect.

This is why the MCP specification warns that tool behavior descriptions should be considered untrusted unless obtained from a trusted server. That warning should change how teams evaluate connections. A tool description is not just UI text. It is an input to an AI system that may decide whether, when, and how to act.

The practical implication is that MCP review should include metadata review. Security teams should inspect:

  • Tool names and descriptions.

  • Argument schemas and defaults.

  • Hidden or excessive instructions in descriptions.

  • Claims that a tool is read-only when it can write.

  • Tools that ask for unrelated context or secrets.

  • Tool outputs that may smuggle instructions back into the conversation.

  • Cross-server interactions, where one server’s output influences use of another server’s tools.

This review cannot be a one-time screenshot. Tool metadata can change across versions, package updates, server responses, and dynamic discovery. Teams should hash or snapshot tool definitions for approved versions, alert on changes, and require re-review when a tool’s behavior or declared schema changes materially.

The broader lesson is simple: in agentic systems, metadata can be executable influence.

The fourth failure mode: supply chain and lifecycle drift

MCP servers are software. That sounds obvious until they are installed like configuration.

Some servers are official or vendor-maintained. Some are community packages. Some are quick internal scripts. Some run locally through stdio. Some run remotely over HTTP. Some are placed behind enterprise gateways. Some are copied from examples and then forgotten. Each path has a different supply-chain and lifecycle risk.

The official MCP Registry helps with discovery and namespace authentication. Its documentation explains that server names use reverse DNS-style namespaces tied to verified GitHub accounts or domains. That is useful for authenticity. But the registry also states that security scanning is delegated to underlying package registries and downstream aggregators, while the registry itself focuses on namespace authentication and metadata hosting. In other words, registry presence should not be mistaken for code assurance.

CoSAI’s MCP security report calls out supply chain and lifecycle failures as a distinct threat category: malicious packages, unvetted community packages, shadow servers, zombie servers, unsigned distributions, typosquatting, and lack of inventory. NSA guidance similarly recommends choosing supported MCP projects where possible, applying stringent code review to MCP server projects, and maintaining internal enrollment processes.

Lifecycle drift is especially important for local MCP use. A developer may install a useful server for a prototype. Six months later, the server remains on the machine, still reachable by an AI host, still holding credentials, still able to access files, but no longer owned or patched. Multiply that across engineering, support, sales, data, and operations teams, and the organization has an invisible integration estate.

This is familiar to anyone who has managed browser extensions, SaaS OAuth apps, CI/CD secrets, or cloud service accounts. MCP is another inventory surface. If security cannot list it, it cannot govern it.

What a security team should inventory

The first practical control is an MCP inventory. Not a one-time spreadsheet, but a living control plane that decides which connections can run in production, which are restricted to experiments, and which should be blocked.

A public registry should be a starting point, not a substitute for internal inventory. Traceforce Atlas is designed for that role: it provides an external reference point for hundreds of MCP servers and their security ratings before teams approve, restrict, or block a server internally.

Figure 5 summarizes the inventory categories that matter. The goal is not bureaucracy. The goal is to make every connection legible before it becomes a path to action.

A useful MCP inventory should include at least the following.

Server identity. Record the server name, namespace, package source, repository, publisher, version, checksum or signature if available, and whether it is official, vendor-supported, community-maintained, or internal.

Business owner. Every connection needs an owner who can explain why it exists, which workflow depends on it, who approves changes, and who can turn it off during an incident.

Runtime location. Note whether the server runs locally, in a container, on a developer workstation, in a managed gateway, in a cloud environment, or as a remote SaaS endpoint. Runtime location affects file access, network exposure, secrets handling, and logging.

Transport and network exposure. Record whether the server uses stdio, streamable HTTP, server-sent events, or another transport. Note binding behavior, reachable interfaces, ingress controls, egress controls, proxying, TLS, and whether the server can access internal networks.

Host and client applications. List which AI hosts can connect to the server. A server approved for a sandbox IDE is not automatically approved for a company-wide chat assistant.

Authentication model. Record how users, agents, and servers authenticate. Identify whether access uses OAuth, static API keys, environment credentials, service accounts, user-delegated tokens, or local OS permissions.

Scopes and permission grants. Capture requested scopes, granted scopes, default scopes, progressive elevation behavior, and whether wildcard or omnibus scopes are present. Link scopes to actual tool categories.

Tool catalog. Store tool names, descriptions, schemas, categories, and risk levels. Classify tools as read, write, destructive, admin, code execution, browser automation, data export, identity management, billing, or secrets-related.

Data classes. Record which data the server can read or write: public, internal, confidential, regulated, customer data, employee data, source code, credentials, financial records, health data, or production operational data.

Downstream systems. Identify every API, database, SaaS app, file path, cloud account, queue, repository, browser session, or internal service the server can touch.

Secrets and token storage. Record where credentials live, who can read them, rotation cadence, token lifetime, refresh-token behavior, and whether secrets may appear in logs, environment variables, prompts, tool outputs, or local config files.

Policy controls. Record which gateway, allowlist, denylist, DLP control, approval workflow, step-up authentication, or per-tool policy applies.

Runtime constraints. Capture sandboxing, containerization, filesystem restrictions, command allowlists, timeouts, output limits, rate limits, memory limits, and network egress restrictions.

Audit and telemetry. Define required logs, trace IDs, retention, SIEM routing, alert rules, and incident queries. If a connection can act but cannot be traced, it should not be treated as production-ready.

Change management. Record review status, last review date, version pinning, update process, metadata change detection, and deprecation plan.

Emergency controls. Every connection needs a kill switch: disable server, revoke token, block egress, remove host access, rotate secrets, or quarantine the runtime.

This inventory should be queryable by risk. Security should be able to answer: show me every MCP connection that can write to production systems; every server with broad scopes; every local server with filesystem access; every tool that can execute code; every connection using static credentials; every server without SIEM logs; every unowned server; every server touching regulated data; every server whose tool metadata changed in the last week.

That is the level of inventory needed when AI-connected tools can act.

Controls that make MCP safer

Inventory tells you what exists. Controls decide what is allowed.

The strongest MCP programs will likely converge on a few patterns.

First, use an allowlist or private registry for approved servers. Public discovery is useful, but production use should flow through a curated path. Security should know the server source, version, owner, risk level, and review status before the connection is available to broad user populations.

A practical operating loop is registry plus scanner plus continuous update. Start from a curated registry, scan the real MCP inventory regularly, and feed any discovered shadow MCP servers back into the registry or control plane so approval status does not drift behind reality. Traceforce’s open-source MCP X-Ray scanner supports this loop by scanning MCP configuration, analyzing tools and secrets, producing SARIF reports, and uploading results to Atlas for centralized tracking. That makes scanner-driven review part of the governance workflow rather than a one-time manual checklist.

Second, separate experimental connections from production connections. A developer’s local prototype should not silently become an enterprise standard. Sandbox hosts, test tenants, and disposable credentials let teams explore without granting durable access to sensitive systems.

Third, classify tools by action level. Read-only, write, destructive, admin, code execution, data export, and identity-impacting tools need different policies. A user who can search documentation should not automatically be able to delete records or rotate infrastructure.

Fourth, prefer least privilege and progressive elevation. The initial connection should carry the minimum scope needed for discovery or low-risk reads. Higher-risk actions should trigger targeted authorization challenges and create explicit audit events. Broad grants should be treated as exceptions.

Fifth, bind tokens to the intended resource and reject token passthrough. The MCP authorization specification requires clients to use resource indicators and servers to validate that tokens were issued for them. It also says servers must not pass through tokens they received from MCP clients to downstream services. This matters because token audience validation is one of the core ways to prevent confused deputy and token misuse patterns.

Sixth, distinguish human identity from agent identity where possible. If downstream logs show only the human user, incident responders may not know whether the human clicked a button, an assistant made a tool call, or an autonomous workflow acted under delegated authority. Agent-aware audit fields and policy decisions make that distinction visible.

Seventh, sandbox execution. Local and remote servers should run with the least filesystem, process, network, and credential access needed. Use containers, OS sandboxing, command allowlists, path restrictions, resource limits, and output limits. Red Hat’s guidance recommends timeouts, output size limits, server-side rate limits, input sanitization, and least-privilege runtime environments. NSA guidance similarly recommends constraining tool execution and validating parameters in context.

Eighth, inspect tool metadata and outputs as untrusted inputs. Tool descriptions, resource content, prompts, and returned data can influence the model. Review them, snapshot them, monitor changes, and scan for suspicious instructions or hidden content. Treat cross-server interactions as a real risk: one server can influence how the model uses another server’s tools.

Ninth, log every action with a trace ID. The trace should connect user, agent, host, server, tool, policy decision, scopes, parameters, downstream target, output, and result. Logs should be forwarded to security-controlled systems quickly enough to support detection and response.

Tenth, design for revocation. If a server is compromised, can the team immediately disable it? Revoke tokens? Rotate secrets? Block egress? Find every user and host that connected? Search every action it took? If not, the connection is not ready for high-risk work.

These controls are not exotic. They are the same secure computing disciplines used for APIs, cloud accounts, SaaS apps, CI/CD, and endpoint software. MCP’s novelty is that these disciplines now need to be applied to AI-connected action paths.

The principle: if it can act, it must be traced

The final security principle is simple enough to become a policy sentence:

If it can act, it must be traced.

This does not mean every AI answer needs enterprise-grade logging. A local brainstorm that calls no tools is not the same as an agent that updates customer records. But once an MCP connection can read private data, write to a system, execute code, call a browser, trigger a workflow, or move information between trust zones, traceability becomes mandatory.

Figure 6 shows the principle as an end-to-end chain. The trace should not begin at the API write. It should begin at the intent and follow the action through policy and execution.

A trace is more than a log line. It is evidence that an action was authorized, bounded, attributable, and reviewable. It lets security teams answer what happened. It lets compliance teams show who approved access. It lets engineers debug failed workflows. It lets product teams understand where friction appears. It lets incident responders contain a compromised connection.

Most importantly, traceability changes behavior before an incident. When teams know every action will be tied to a principal, scope, policy, tool, and result, they design narrower tools. They avoid broad tokens. They create clearer approvals. They remove unused servers. They stop treating local prototypes as invisible infrastructure.

MCP will likely become a durable part of the AI application stack because the need is real. Models are more useful when they can reach context and act through tools. Organizations will not give that up. The goal is not to block MCP. The goal is to make MCP connections governable.

That starts by naming the boundary. An MCP connection is not “just a connector.” It is a delegated action path between an AI system and something the organization cares about. It deserves the same scrutiny as any path that can access data, modify state, or execute code.

Security teams do not need to slow every experiment to a crawl. They do need a line between exploration and production. They need an inventory that shows what exists. They need least-privilege scopes and per-tool controls. They need runtime containment. They need metadata review. They need audit trails that connect intent to action. And they need the authority to say that any connection without ownership, limits, and traceability stays out of sensitive environments.

The future of AI tooling will not be defined only by smarter models. It will be defined by whether organizations can safely give those models useful reach.

MCP is one of the clearest tests of that discipline. Every connection is a new trust boundary. Every tool is a potential action. Every broad permission is future blast radius. Every missing log is a future blind spot.

If it can act, it must be traced.

Sources and further reading

  • Model Context Protocol specification

  • MCP Security Best Practices

  • MCP Authorization specification

  • NSA: Model Context Protocol Security Design Considerations

  • CoSAI: Model Context Protocol Security

  • Red Hat: MCP security logging and runtime measures

  • OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

  • Invariant Labs: MCP tool poisoning attacks

  • Traceforce Atlas public MCP registry: https://atlas.traceforce.co/

  • Traceforce MCP X-Ray open-source scanner: https://github.com/traceforce/mcp-xray

  • Unit 42: Prompt injection attack vectors through MCP sampling

  • MCP Registry trust and security documentation

item.title: The Missing Control Loop for AI Agents: Intent, Evidence, and Replay
item.description: The OpenAI Build Week build story behind CausalGate, from intent contracts to evidence-backed replay
item.dc:creator: Ken Huang
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI Build Week 2026 submission note: I wrote this article as the public build story for CausalGate’s Developer Tools entry. The project was submitted July 19, 2026, before the July 21 deadline. Official submission: https://devpost.com/software/causalgate

An AI agent can produce a reasonable answer while its tools do the wrong thing. It can read protected data, call a destination outside the approved scope, or complete the visible task through an execution path nobody intended. A transcript may still look fine.

I built CausalGate for that gap. It records the agent's declared intent, captures ordered execution evidence, identifies the point where action diverged, applies intent-based authorization, and reruns the same scenario under protection. The result is not a generic risk score. It is a causal record and a scoped release decision.

This post has two parts. The product story, architecture, demo, and adoption paths are free. The paid section contains the practical evaluation runbook I use to decide whether an agent change is ready to promote.

You can watch the complete 2 minute 56 second demo on YouTube, inspect the public MIT-licensed repository, or run the deterministic demo without an API key.

The problem is not another bad answer

Most agent evaluation still concentrates on model output. Did the response follow instructions? Was it helpful? Did it contain unsafe text? Those questions matter, but they stop before the tools begin to create effects.

The harder question is operational: did the execution remain inside the authority that the user, organization, and runtime actually granted? That requires more than a final transcript. It requires the original intent contract, tool arguments, policy decisions, data classifications, destinations, effects, and links between each claim and the event that supports it.

Figure 1 illustrates The Intent Visibility Gap. It shows why a successful-looking answer cannot prove that the underlying execution respected purpose, data boundaries, or destination limits.

Figure 1: The Intent Visibility Gap

Traditional logs usually tell you that a tool ran. They do not always tell you whether that action was necessary for the user's purpose, whether the agent was authorized to take it, or which earlier decision made the harmful effect possible. CausalGate treats those questions as first-class product behavior.

What CausalGate records

A run begins with a typed intent contract. The contract identifies the subject, purpose, allowed actions, protected resources, expected effects, and limits. CausalGate then records normalized events as the agent calls tools and receives policy decisions.

Deterministic detectors analyze that evidence. They do not ask a model to invent a verdict. Each finding points back to supporting event IDs and explains the divergence in concrete terms. The system then assembles an Intent Causal Record that ties contract, execution, findings, authorization, and limitations together.

Figure 2 illustrates Evidence Becomes a Causal Record. The important design choice is the chain of custody: every conclusion remains connected to the contract and ordered events that produced it.

Figure 2: Evidence Becomes a Causal Record

This makes the product useful for more than incident review. The same record can support QA, security review, release approval, and audit evidence. A reviewer can challenge a finding without having to trust an opaque score.

The demo includes a synthetic vulnerable scenario with eight evidence-linked findings. It is intentionally deterministic, so judges and developers can reproduce the same result without a paid API or external system. Optional GPT-5.6 analysis is explicit, ephemeral BYOK. The key is sent only for that request and is not stored by CausalGate.

Intent-Based Access Control

Role-based access answers whether an identity can call a tool. CausalGate adds a second question: can this agent take this action, for this purpose, on this resource, at this destination, with these effects, in the current runtime context?

The authorization engine normalizes tool calls against an ontology and evaluates an intersection of identity, agent authority, intent grant, organization policy, and runtime context. It records allow, deny, and approval-required outcomes as evidence. Unknown mappings fail closed.

Figure 3 illustrates Authority Is an Intersection. No single credential or plausible tool call is enough; the action proceeds only when every required authority boundary agrees.

Figure 3: Authority Is an Intersection

This matters because agent failures often look individually legitimate. A read may be allowed, and an outbound send may be allowed, yet the combination may violate the declared purpose. Purpose and effect have to remain attached to authority throughout the run.

Replay before release

Finding a problem is only half the control loop. Teams still need to know whether the proposed protection actually changes behavior without hiding evidence or breaking the intended task.

CausalGate reruns the same scenario with protection enabled. It compares baseline and replay findings, preserves the authorization record, and emits a scoped recommendation. In the included scenario, the vulnerable run produces eight findings while the protected replay produces zero, leading to a promote recommendation for that tested scope.

Figure 4 illustrates Replay Turns a Fix Into Evidence. A fix earns promotion by changing the observed execution under the same scenario, not by sounding convincing in a review comment.

Figure 4: Replay Turns a Fix Into Evidence

Replay does not prove universal safety. It proves something narrower and more useful: this protection changed this scenario, under this contract and runtime, with this evidence. CausalGate keeps that boundary explicit instead of converting one passing run into a broad guarantee.

SDK and SaaS are two views of the same engine

The Python SDK is for teams that need control inside the agent runtime. They install the package, wrap execution, declare the intent contract, record events, authorize tool calls, generate the causal record, and use replay results in CI or a release workflow.

The smallest adoption path remains familiar:

from causalgate import CausalGate

gate = CausalGate()
run = gate.start_run(contract)
gate.record(run, event)
report = gate.analyze(run)

The contract and event objects are typed, and the engine produces deterministic evidence. The likely failure point is incomplete instrumentation: if a tool bypasses the recorder or authorizer, the record cannot claim complete mediation. CausalGate reports that limitation rather than hiding it.

The SaaS version uses the same engine as a shared control plane. Teams send normalized, tenant-authorized evidence to a hosted service, review causal records in the UI, compare baseline and replay runs, manage policy versions, and connect promote or block decisions to deployment systems. The current repository is an alpha reference implementation and judge profile, not a claim that multi-tenant production hardening is finished.

Figure 5 illustrates One Engine, Two Adoption Paths. The SDK optimizes for embedded enforcement and developer control; SaaS optimizes for shared review, governance, and evidence retention across many agents and teams.

Figure 5: One Engine, Two Adoption Paths

This split also creates a clean privacy boundary. Sensitive raw payloads can remain inside the customer's runtime while the hosted layer receives normalized events, digests, redacted evidence, and explicit limitations. Production SaaS still requires durable tenant storage, workload identity, shared atomic permit state, private workers, and managed audit retention. Those boundaries are documented rather than implied.

What Codex and GPT-5.6 changed

This was not a one-prompt wrapper. During the Build Week submission period, I used Codex and GPT-5.6 to turn an existing technical direction into a coherent, testable product. The work included tracing the PRD and architecture into the running system, fixing authorization-evidence corruption, making optional live analysis fail safely, closing SQLite connection leaks, adding regression tests, clarifying the SDK and SaaS boundaries, completing browser QA, preparing the public deployment, and documenting where the implementation still differs from the product design. The dated commits and primary-session evidence are linked from the Devpost submission and repository build log.

I used Codex as an engineering collaborator across product design, architecture, implementation, debugging, documentation, browser QA, and release preparation. The useful part was not raw code generation. It was the loop: inspect the PRD and architecture, trace the implementation, reproduce failures, patch the smallest responsible surface, run the full suite, and compare the product against the written contract.

GPT-5.6 was used where broader reasoning mattered, including the causal model, authorization ontology, product boundary, SDK and SaaS framing, and the review of gaps between the PRD and implementation. Deterministic code still owns enforcement and release decisions. Optional live GPT-5.6 analysis adds semantic investigation, but it does not replace the recorded evidence or policy engine.

That distinction is important. I do not want a second model to declare the first model safe. I want models to help humans understand evidence while deterministic controls retain authority.

A release gate you can inspect

The repository currently passes 80 backend tests with 90 percent coverage, 9 UI tests, a production TypeScript build, and browser QA. The public demo runs with synthetic data and no account requirement. Docker and Cloud Run deployment profiles use a single instance because the judge profile stores SQLite state locally and keeps a process-local permit ledger.

Figure 6 illustrates The Release Decision. The final output remains operational: promote the tested scope, hold for missing evidence, or block because a material divergence remains.

Figure 6: The Release Decision

The biggest product lesson is simple. Agent safety becomes actionable when intent, authority, evidence, replay, and release decisions live in one loop. Without that loop, teams collect impressive traces and still make release decisions by intuition.

For paid subscribers: the practical release runbook continues below.

It turns the architecture into seven concrete checks for contract quality, complete mediation, vulnerable baselines, evidence links, controlled replay, scoped decisions, and durable records.

Subscribe to unlock the runbook: https://kenhuangus.substack.com/subscribe?coupon=302342d9.

item.title: Proof-of-Control Assurance Framework for Universal Commerce Protocol Agentic Commerce
item.description: Verifiable Governance for Agentic Commerce at Institutional Scale
item.dc:creator: Ken Huang
item.content:encoded:
This framework builds on the work of the Proof-of-Control Initiative at the Advanced AI Society, the industry body for verifiable AI, where I serve as co-chair. If you want to help define what verifiable agentic commerce should require, or follow this work as it develops, you can learn more and get involved here.

We try to define a Proof-of-Control assurance framework for the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP).

Protocol source basis:

  • Repository: universal-commerce-protocol/ucp

  • Branch reviewed: main

  • Main commit reviewed: cc3608a

  • Main commit date: 2026-07-17 17:54:23 UTC

  • Main commit subject: feat: shopping permalink capability (#523)

Release status: v2026-04-08 remains the latest tagged release. This review also covers unreleased main-branch changes through cc3608a.

Current primary sources:

  • UCP technical specification and repository

  • Google: Under the Hood: Universal Commerce Protocol

  • Shopify Engineering: Building the Universal Commerce Protocol

  • Ilya Grigorik: Millions of merchants speak UCP

  • Ilya Grigorik and Tobi Lütke: UCP and protocol design

  • Shopify developer documentation: Build commerce agents with UCP

  • Shopify Spring '26: Agentic commerce for every developer

Related research and analysis:

  • Ken Huang: Google and Shopify's UCP Just Won Agentic Commerce

  • IMF: How Agentic AI Will Reshape Payments

  • Strabo: Declarative Specification and Implementation of Agentic Interaction Protocols

  • Zero-Trust Runtime Verification for AP2

The purpose of this document is not to redefine UCP. The purpose is to specify what must be provable for UCP-enabled agentic commerce to be defensible in enterprise, regulated, insured, and high-value transaction environments.

Executive Summary

The Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) is an open, capability-negotiation protocol for agentic commerce. It gives AI agents, apps, search surfaces, procurement systems, merchants, and payment providers a shared way to discover what each party supports; negotiate compatible services, capabilities, extensions, schemas, payment handlers, and transports; and carry a transaction from product discovery and cart building through checkout, identity linking, orders, and post-purchase events.

UCP matters because agentic commerce is a many-to-many coordination problem, not merely a checkout button. A common, extensible protocol can replace bespoke integrations, preserve merchant-controlled rules and merchant-of-record responsibilities, and allow diverse agents and businesses to interoperate without forcing commerce into one platform's proprietary workflow. As argued in my April 2026 Substack analysis, UCP's broad governance coalition and full-lifecycle design make it a plausible shared coordination layer for the emerging agentic-commerce ecosystem.

Since UCP's launch, the ecosystem has moved from launch specification toward broader implementation: Shopify now documents self-serve developer access to UCP and Catalog surfaces spanning products from millions of merchants, and protocol governance and technical participation have expanded. This is an implementation and ecosystem milestone, not a new tagged protocol version: v2026-04-08 remains the latest tag, while newer security and capability work resides on main.

UCP therefore changes the trust boundary in ecommerce. In a traditional web checkout, the buyer directly interacts with a merchant-controlled UI. In UCP-enabled commerce, an AI agent may discover products, build a cart, negotiate checkout state, transmit signals, select a payment handler, submit payment credentials, or receive order events on the buyer's behalf.

Openness and interoperability, however, do not by themselves establish trust. A protocol can be open while the evidence needed to evaluate an agent's authority, a merchant's advertised state, or a payment decision remains controlled by one platform. Independent and open verification is therefore essential: auditors, regulators, insurers, counterparties, and users should be able to validate portable evidence using public schemas and verification rules, without relying on the vendor that executed the transaction or on inaccessible proprietary telemetry. That requires cryptographically bound identities and mandates, signed and content-digested messages, preserved negotiation and checkout state, tamper-evident event histories, and reproducible policy checks. The result is not the elimination of risk; it is a reduction in unilateral trust and a defensible basis for accountability, dispute resolution, and cross-platform governance.

That creates the central institutional governance question:

Can every material UCP commerce action be independently proven to have been authorized, constrained, executed, and recorded according to the active business profile, platform profile, negotiated capability set, payment handler, identity scope, checkout state, and user mandate?

The Proof-of-Control answer is to shift assurance from platform promises and after-the-fact audit reconstruction to independently verifiable evidence generated at the moment of action. That evidence can include HTTP Message Signatures, content digests, JWK key discovery, idempotency keys, signed negotiation transcripts, Merkle-anchored event logs, runtime attestation, formal verification, AP2 mandates, HSM-backed signing, and privacy-preserving compliance proofs.

UCP already includes several important security primitives. This framework turns those primitives into an institutional assurance profile.

Figure 1 illustrates the new trust boundary. The agent may coordinate the transaction, but an independent verifier must be able to reconstruct authority and state without trusting the agent's own account of events.

Figure 1: Independent Verification Boundary

Scope

This document covers:

  • UCP discovery, negotiation, identity, payment, checkout, order, signal, and mandate surfaces.

  • Cloud Security Alliance’s Agentic Threat Modeling MAESTRO-layer threats that apply to UCP-enabled agentic commerce.

  • Proof mechanisms that provide tamper-resistant evidence of control implementation and operation.

  • UCP-specific control requirements for enterprise and regulated deployments.

  • Implementation phases and success metrics for Proof-of-Control adoption.

This document does not claim that proof mechanisms eliminate all risk. It does not prove that an AI model made the best recommendation, that a product is fairly ranked, that merchant data is truthful, or that every future attack is covered. It establishes what can be independently verified about protocol state, authority, execution, and evidence.

Section 1: UCP Protocol Grounding

This section summarizes the UCP protocol surfaces that matter for Proof-of-Control.

1.1 Participants

UCP defines several participants:

Table 1 shows that UCP distributes control across five distinct parties rather than placing it in a single agent. The assurance implication is decisive: identity, delegation, credential custody, payment authorization, and merchant state each require evidence from the party that actually controls that fact, so an agent's own transaction narrative is never sufficient.

Table 1: UCP Participants and Proof-of-Control Concerns

1.2 Discovery Profiles

UCP uses discovery profiles as the root of capability and key discovery.

Business profiles are hosted at:

/.well-known/ucp

Platform profiles are advertised per request through the UCP-Agent header:

UCP-Agent: profile="https://platform.example/.well-known/ucp"

Profiles contain:

  • ucp.version

  • ucp.services

  • ucp.capabilities

  • ucp.payment_handlers

  • optional ucp.supported_versions for business profiles

  • keys[] in JWK format

Proof-of-Control implication: the profile is the first evidence object in a UCP session. A high-assurance deployment should preserve a signed or hash-pinned snapshot of the business profile and platform profile used for each commerce session.

1.3 Profile Requirements and Fetch Controls

UCP requires profiles to be reliably hosted over HTTPS. Profile endpoints must not use redirects. Implementations must reject non-HTTPS profile URLs and must not follow profile-fetch redirects.

UCP also recognizes that dynamic profile discovery creates operational risk. Implementations should use bounded profile caches, rate limits, negative caching, and asynchronous discovery where appropriate.

Proof-of-Control implication: profile fetching is both a discovery function and a security boundary. The fetch event, validation result, cache key, profile hash, and selected signing key should be recorded.

1.4 Services, Capabilities, and Extensions

UCP organizes commerce features into services and capabilities.

Important UCP capabilities include:

  • dev.ucp.shopping.catalog.search

  • dev.ucp.shopping.catalog.lookup

  • dev.ucp.shopping.cart

  • dev.ucp.shopping.checkout

  • dev.ucp.shopping.order

  • dev.ucp.common.identity_linking

Important UCP extensions include:

  • dev.ucp.shopping.fulfillment

  • dev.ucp.shopping.discount

  • dev.ucp.shopping.buyer_consent

  • dev.ucp.shopping.ap2_mandate

Extensions compose onto parent capabilities through extends and JSON Schema composition. UCP prunes orphaned extensions if the parent capability is not in the negotiated intersection.

Proof-of-Control implication: a UCP session needs a signed negotiation transcript recording which service, capability, extension, version, schema, and transport were active.

Figure 2 shows why UCP is a negotiation protocol rather than a single checkout API. Profiles advertise possibilities, the parties compute a supported intersection, schemas define the active contract, and incompatible cases escalate instead of being improvised by the model.

Figure 2: UCP Capability Negotiation

1.5 Namespace Governance

UCP uses reverse-domain names for capabilities and services:

{reverse-domain}.{service}.{capability}

Examples:

  • dev.ucp.shopping.checkout

  • dev.ucp.common.identity_linking

  • com.example.payments.installments

A capability must declare a schema URL; services and payment handlers declare one when their transport or handler defines it. The schema URL is the authority anchor: its HTTPS host must match the reverse-domain namespace authority, and platforms must validate that binding before fetching it and must not follow redirects. A spec URL is optional, must use HTTPS when present, and may be hosted outside the namespace authority because it is documentation rather than the fetched validation artifact.

Proof-of-Control implication: schema-authority validation, safe fetch controls, and the hash of each fetched schema should be explicit evidence events. Record spec URLs for traceability, but do not mischaracterize their origin as a UCP trust anchor.

1.6 Versioning

UCP uses date-based protocol versions in YYYY-MM-DD format. Public profiles must not advertise non-date versions such as draft. Businesses that support older versions should use supported_versions to map each supported version to a complete version-specific profile. Version-specific profiles are leaf documents and must not contain supported_versions.

Proof-of-Control implication: protocol version, capability version, extension version, and schema hash should be bound into the session evidence bundle.

1.7 Transport Bindings

UCP supports multiple transports:

  • REST using OpenAPI

  • MCP using OpenRPC over streamable HTTP

  • A2A through Agent Card style integration

  • Embedded protocol using OpenRPC

Proof-of-Control implication: the selected transport changes the evidence surface. REST and MCP over HTTP can use the same HTTP Message Signature foundation. Embedded and A2A flows require equivalent evidence binding for handoff, message origin, and session state.

1.8 HTTP Message Signatures

UCP defines HTTP Message Signatures using RFC 9421 for HTTP-based transports. The shared foundation includes:

  • Signature-Input

  • Signature

  • Content-Digest

  • ES256 required for verification

  • ES384 and Ed25519 optional; unsupported algorithms are skipped per signature resolution

  • JWK public keys in profile keys[]

  • Content-Digest over raw body bytes

  • idempotency keys for replay protection at the business layer

UCP states that platforms should sign requests when using HTTP Message Signatures, while alternative authentication such as OAuth, API keys, or mTLS may be used. Webhook notifications must be signed. Optional Web Bot Auth interoperability adds Signature-Agent-based key resolution and stricter signature parameters without replacing the baseline UCP-Agent path.

Proof-of-Control implication: institutional deployments should make signatures mandatory for every state-changing UCP action and should preserve verification results.

1.9 Catalog

UCP catalog capabilities support product discovery through search and lookup. Catalog operations can use product and variant IDs that later appear in checkout line_items[].item.id. UCP distinguishes catalog context from final checkout enforcement: catalog responses can be context-sensitive and should not be treated as the final authority for eligibility, tax, fulfillment, or payment.

Proof-of-Control implication: product, price, inventory, and variant data used by agents should be signed or hash-anchored at ingestion and retrieval time.

1.10 Cart

UCP cart supports pre-checkout basket building. A cart may be converted into a checkout by providing cart_id in a Create Checkout request. When checkout is initialized by cart_id, the business must use cart contents and ignore overlapping fields in the checkout payload. If an incomplete checkout already exists for the cart, the business must return the existing checkout session rather than create a new one.

Proof-of-Control implication: cart-to-checkout binding is a critical evidence point. The cart snapshot, checkout ID, and idempotency key should be linked.

1.11 Checkout

The Checkout capability is the central UCP transaction primitive. UCP states that checkout must be finalized manually by the user through a trusted UI unless the AP2 Mandates extension is supported.

Checkout statuses include:

  • incomplete

  • requires_escalation

  • ready_for_complete

  • complete_in_progress

  • completed

  • canceled

When status is requires_escalation, the business must provide continue_url. The platform must use continue_url when checkout status is requires_escalation. Businesses must include at least one message with severity requires_buyer_input or requires_buyer_review when returning requires_escalation. After checkout reaches completed, it is considered immutable.

Proof-of-Control implication: checkout state must be treated as a formal state machine. Any bypass of requires_escalation is a control failure.

1.12 Payment Handlers

UCP payment handlers are specifications, not entities. They define how payment instruments are acquired and processed. Businesses and platforms advertise handlers and available_instruments; the checkout response provides runtime handler configuration. UCP states that the available_instruments in the checkout response is authoritative for that checkout. Platforms must not use instrument types or constraints that contradict it.

The payment-handler guide also notes that availableinstruments is optional. When absent, the handler places no restrictions on instrument types and supports the full set defined by its handler schema. A checkout submission must contain exactly one instrument unless dev.ucp.shopping.splitpayments is active; when active, the business-defined allowed combinations and atomic failure/reversal rules apply.

Payment-handler specifications should define binding, credential types, expiration, common failures, and processing rules. Binding means a cryptographic or logical association between a payment instrument, a specific checkout transaction, and business identity.

Proof-of-Control implication: high-assurance deployments should require explicit instrument constraints, credential binding, expiration, and signed handler provenance.

1.13 Identity Linking

UCP identity linking uses OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE as the baseline and lets a platform obtain authorization to act for a user at a business. Businesses declare UCP scopes in config.scopes under dev.ucp.common.identity_linking. The current main branch also allows businesses to advertise trusted external identity providers and accept short-lived, single-use JWT authorization grants; the business must validate issuer, exact audience, signature, expiry, required claims, and jti replay state before issuing its own access token.

Important identity-linking controls include:

  • PKCE with S256

  • issuer (iss) validation to prevent mix-up attacks

  • exact redirect_uri matching

  • WWW-Authenticate: Bearer challenges

  • identity_required and insufficient_scope handling

  • token revocation

  • scope derivation from negotiated capabilities

  • user identity tokens in the Authorization: Bearer header

Proof-of-Control implication: scope derivation, consent, token validation, revocation, and operation-to-scope mapping should be auditable.

1.14 Signals

UCP signals support fraud prevention, risk assessment, authorization, and abuse prevention. Signal values must not be buyer-asserted claims. Platforms provide signals based on direct observation or by relaying independently verifiable third-party attestations.

Proof-of-Control implication: signals should be minimized, provenance-bound, and retention-controlled. Third-party signal attestations should be signed.

1.15 Attribution

UCP attribution is informational and optionally provided by the platform. UCP does not prescribe attribution models, windows, or assignment logic. The field must not affect negotiation.

Proof-of-Control implication: attribution data may be useful for analytics, but it should not be treated as authorization evidence without additional controls.

1.16 Buyer Consent

The Buyer Consent extension now supports cart and checkout and models consent as reverse-domain purposes with optional, more-specific segments. Businesses advertise the complete supported option set and current source/value; platforms must use the advertised labels and content when presenting choices and must not invent unsupported purposes. The protocol communicates consent state and blocks checkout completion when confirmed choices have unmet data dependencies, but downstream data-use, retention, sharing, and deletion enforcement remains a separate business-policy obligation.

Proof-of-Control implication: consent transport must be linked to separate policy enforcement evidence for data use, retention, sharing, and deletion.

1.17 AP2 Mandates

The AP2 Mandates extension, dev.ucp.shopping.ap2_mandate, adds cryptographic mandate support for autonomous commerce.

When the AP2 extension is negotiated:

  • The business must include ap2.merchant_authorization in checkout responses.

  • The platform must verify the business signature before presenting terms.

  • The business must not accept complete_checkout without ap2.checkout_mandate.

  • Mandates are SD-JWT credentials with key binding.

  • Two mandate artifacts are required: a checkout mandate and a payment mandate.

  • The checkout mandate is placed at ap2.checkout_mandate.

  • The payment mandate is placed in payment.instruments[*].credential.token.

  • AP2 uses JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) for durable signature artifacts.

Proof-of-Control implication: AP2 is the UCP-native path for non-repudiable autonomous commerce. Autonomous completion without AP2 or trusted deterministic UI should be treated as high risk.

1.18 Order Events

The Order capability allows businesses to push order lifecycle updates to platforms through webhooks. Webhook payloads must be signed. The platform must verify that the signer is authorized to send events for the referenced order by matching the signer profile to the order's business.

UCP order events send the full order entity, not only deltas.

Proof-of-Control implication: signed order events should be anchored into an append-only event stream linked to the originating checkout and business profile.

1.19 Current Maturity and Post-Release Changes

The latest tagged protocol release remains v2026-04-08. The reviewed main branch at cc3608a is 65 commits ahead of the document's previous May 6 baseline and contains material work that is not yet represented by a newer tag. Production deployments should pin the protocol and capability versions they implement, validate the advertised schemas for that version, and treat main-branch additions as pre-release until formally tagged.

  • Profile and transport security: the canonical public-key field is now top-level keys[] (an RFC 7517 JWK Set). Every verifier must support ES256; Ed25519 is optional. A request may opt into Web Bot Auth interoperability with Signature-Agent, additional covered components, key-thumbprint binding, and created/expires parameters. Default UCP key resolution through UCP-Agent remains supported.

  • Identity linking: direct OAuth 2.0 with PKCE remains the baseline. Main also specifies an accelerated identity-provider flow using short-lived, single-use JWT authorization grants, exact audience binding, jti replay prevention, and business-issued access tokens; raw upstream identity-provider tokens must not be relayed directly to a business.

  • Buyer consent: the extension now decorates cart and checkout, supports reverse-domain purposes and nested segments, makes the business-advertised option set authoritative, and blocks completion when a confirmed choice has unmet data dependencies. It still does not by itself prove downstream policy enforcement.

  • Loyalty: dev.ucp.common.loyalty can decorate catalog, cart, and checkout to expose memberships, tiers, benefits, and rewards. Redeemable balances and stored value remain the responsibility of payment instruments or a future redemption capability.

  • Split payments: dev.ucp.shopping.split_payments permits multiple instruments only when negotiated. Businesses advertise allowed combinations; submissions are ordered by allocation priority, and failed partial processing must be reversed so an incomplete split does not leave the buyer charged.

  • Shopping permalinks: dev.ucp.shopping.permalink defines a browser-addressable GET intent that initializes shopping state and resolves through a 303 redirect. Loading a permalink is never authorization to place an order, charge payment, or complete checkout; continue_to and field-path inputs require strict server-side validation.

  • Industry expansion and governance: the public project now identifies co-development groups for shopping, lodging, and food, while the roadmap describes food and lodging specifications as work in progress. Stripe joined the Governing Council, and Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Salesforce, and Stripe representatives joined the expanded Technical Committee.

Shopify's current developer implementation is self-serve: developers register an agent profile and use UCP-compliant MCP endpoints for discovery, cart, checkout, and order flows. Shopify describes Catalog API as exposing billions of products from millions of merchants, but authority is tiered. Anonymous and signed agents cannot call complete_checkout or order tools; those actions require token-tier authorization and the relevant scopes. The merchant remains the merchant of record.

Proof-of-Control implication: evidence bundles must record whether a behavior came from a tagged protocol release, an advertised version-specific profile, an unreleased main-branch capability, or a Shopify-specific implementation policy. Conformance to UCP does not imply entitlement to every platform's highest-trust operation.

Related 2026 research reinforces the control boundary used here. The IMF separates probabilistic intent and orchestration from deterministic authorization/control and settlement. Strabo shows that UCP checkout interactions can be represented as a formal declarative protocol while retaining interoperability. Separate AP2 runtime analysis argues that signatures and expiry alone are insufficient under retries and concurrency without explicit context binding and consume-once enforcement. These are research findings and analytical frameworks, not normative UCP requirements.

Section 2: The UCP Provability/Verifiability Gap

UCP defines protocol interoperability and includes several important security mechanisms. However, institutional adoption requires stronger evidence requirements than baseline protocol conformance.

2.1 What UCP Already Provides

UCP already provides:

  • Machine-readable business and platform profiles.

  • JWK key discovery through profiles.

  • RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures for HTTP-based transports.

  • Content-Digest over raw body bytes.

  • Idempotency keys for state-changing operations.

  • HTTPS-only profile and communication requirements.

  • Capability, extension, and version negotiation.

  • Reverse-domain namespace governance.

  • Schema-origin binding for capabilities, services, and payment handlers.

  • OAuth 2.0 identity linking with PKCE and issuer validation.

  • Checkout state lifecycle and escalation rules.

  • Payment-handler negotiation.

  • Signed order webhooks.

  • Optional AP2 mandates for autonomous and high-value transactions.

2.2 What UCP Does Not Prove by Itself

Baseline UCP does not automatically prove:

  • That historical profiles were not changed after a dispute.

  • That every state-changing request was signed.

  • That every material response was signed and retained.

  • That the negotiated capability set was preserved as an audit artifact.

  • That schema documents fetched during negotiation were hash-pinned.

  • That the agent runtime or merchant runtime was untampered.

  • That a payment handler implementation matched its specification.

  • That buyer consent was enforced after it was transmitted.

  • That attribution was accurate or compliant.

  • That catalog data was accurate, fresh, complete, or unbiased.

  • That an LLM recommendation was safe, fair, or optimal.

2.3 Proof-of-Control Objective

Proof-of-Control closes the evidentiary gap by requiring that high-value UCP actions produce independently verifiable evidence at the time of action.

The target state is:

  • Profiles are authenticated, hash-pinned, and retained.

  • Negotiation decisions are recorded in signed transcripts.

  • State-changing messages are signed.

  • Checkout state transitions are tamper-evident.

  • AP2 mandates or trusted UI review prove authorization.

  • Payment credentials are bound to checkout, merchant, handler, amount, currency, and expiry.

  • Identity scopes are linked to operations.

  • Order events are signed and append-only.

  • Runtime and supply-chain controls are attestable.

Section 3: Proof-of-Control Principles

Principle 1: Evidence Must Exist Before a Dispute

Contracts create remedies after a violation. Proof-of-Control creates evidence while the transaction occurs. UCP systems should not depend on reconstructing authority from mutable logs months later.

Principle 2: Authority Must Be Scoped

Agent authority must be scoped to the active UCP profile, negotiated capabilities, identity scopes, checkout state, payment handler, and mandate terms. A general platform identity is not enough.

Principle 3: Negotiation Must Be Auditable

UCP's capability negotiation determines what an agent and business can safely do together. The selected protocol version, service, transport, capabilities, extensions, schemas, payment handlers, and identity scopes must be recorded as a session artifact.

Principle 4: Checkout State Must Be Enforced

The checkout lifecycle is a control surface. requires_escalation means the platform must hand off through continue_url. Programmatic completion must be limited to valid states and valid authority.

Principle 5: Payment Must Be Bound

Payment credentials must be bound to the intended business, checkout, handler, amount, currency, and expiration. A valid credential that can be replayed against another merchant or checkout is not sufficient.

Principle 6: Consent Transport Is Not Consent Enforcement

UCP can carry buyer consent. Proof-of-Control must show that consent state was actually applied to data handling, retention, sharing, and deletion behavior.

Principle 7: Logs Must Be Tamper-Evident

If the system being audited can rewrite its own evidence, the evidence is not institutionally defensible. UCP action logs should be signed and anchored.

Principle 8: Proof Has Limits

Digital signatures prove origin and integrity, not business correctness. Runtime attestation proves measured code ran, not that the code was bug-free. Formal verification proves properties against a specification, not that the specification captures every real-world risk.
