Section 6: MAESTRO Layered Threat and Control Model

Layer 1: Foundation Model Security

UCP relevance: UCP does not define model internals. However, platforms may use models to search catalogs, rank products, select variants, interpret merchant messages, decide when to escalate, or assemble checkout inputs.

Primary threats:

  • Prompt injection causes an agent to ignore UCP messages or checkout state.

  • Model or policy version changes commerce behavior without approval.

  • Ranking manipulation changes product discovery outcomes.

  • Agent treats provisional catalog context as final checkout authority.

  • Agent completes checkout when buyer review or AP2 authorization is required.

Controls:

  • Sign model, policy, prompt, and tool manifests used for commerce flows.

  • Bind commerce-agent policy to UCP states, especially requires_escalation and ready_for_complete.

  • Commit to evaluation datasets for UCP-specific safety tests.

  • Attest model-serving and policy-enforcement runtime for high-risk flows.

  • Require deterministic policy enforcement outside the LLM for checkout completion, payment, and identity decisions.

Proof evidence:

  • Signed model manifest.

  • Signed commerce policy manifest.

  • Runtime attestation report.

  • Evaluation commitment and result signature.

  • Decision log linking recommendation, UCP state, and authority basis.

Limits: This does not prove the model's recommendation is optimal, fair, or safe for all novel prompts.

Layer 2: Data Operations Security

UCP relevance: UCP catalog, cart, checkout, buyer, context, signal, attribution, consent, and order data shape agent decisions.

Primary threats:

  • Poisoned catalog data causes wrong product selection.

  • Stale price or inventory data misleads the agent.

  • Product or variant ID mismatch causes checkout of the wrong item.

  • Signals are buyer-asserted rather than observed or attested.

  • Consent state is transmitted but not enforced.

  • Attribution identifiers are over-collected or retained too long.

Controls:

  • Sign product feeds, catalog indexes, inventory updates, and price updates.

  • Hash-chain product, price, inventory, and vector-store update logs.

  • Treat checkout response as authoritative for final price, eligibility, fulfillment, tax, and payment constraints.

  • Validate that signals use reverse-domain names and are observed or signed.

  • Bind consent state to data-use policy enforcement.

  • Minimize signal and attribution retention according to policy.

Proof evidence:

  • Signed catalog manifest.

  • Merkle proof for product state at recommendation time.

  • Signed signal attestation.

  • Consent-to-policy enforcement log.

  • Checkout response hash.

  • Data retention proof or deletion certificate.

Limits: This proves data integrity and provenance, not truthfulness, commercial fairness, or absence of bias.

Layer 3: Agent Framework Security

UCP relevance: This layer covers the agent loop, capability negotiation, schema composition, cart updates, checkout state transitions, payment-handler selection, and tool calls.

Primary threats:

  • Platform invokes a capability outside the negotiated intersection.

  • Malicious extension spoofs a UCP namespace or schema origin.

  • Orphaned extension remains active after parent capability pruning.

  • Schema substitution changes request or response semantics.

  • Agent bypasses requires_escalation.

  • Duplicate requests create duplicate orders or charges.

  • Valid tool inputs are used for unauthorized business outcomes.

Controls:

  • Validate reverse-domain capability names.

  • Enforce schema URL authority binding before fetch; require HTTPS for spec URLs.

  • Verify extension extends and requires compatibility.

  • Formally verify or exhaustively test the capability intersection and extension pruning algorithm.

  • Compose schemas from negotiated capabilities and validate all requests and responses against the active schema.

  • Treat checkout as a formal state machine.

  • Sign idempotency keys for all state-changing actions.

  • Preserve a signed negotiation transcript.

Proof evidence:

  • Signed negotiation transcript.

  • Profile hashes.

  • Schema hashes.

  • Active capability and extension list.

  • Checkout state transition log.

  • Idempotency verification record.

  • Tool-call authorization log.

Limits: Formal verification applies to bounded logic, not open-ended LLM reasoning.

Layer 4: Deployment and Infrastructure Security

UCP relevance: This layer covers REST, MCP, A2A, embedded flows, profile fetching, schema fetching, gateways, signing keys, checkout services, payment handlers, and PSP adapters.

Primary threats:

  • SSRF or resource exhaustion through malicious profile URLs.

  • Redirect-based profile substitution.

  • Profile cache poisoning.

  • API gateway reserializes JSON and invalidates Content-Digest.

  • Signing keys are stolen or misused.

  • Payment-handler implementation differs from its specification.

  • Embedded checkout introduces UI or state confusion.

Controls:

  • Enforce HTTPS-only profiles and no redirects.

  • Use bounded profile caches, rate limits, and negative caching.

  • HSM- or KMS-protect signing keys.

  • Ensure gateways preserve raw body bytes used for Content-Digest.

  • Use runtime attestation for high-risk agent, checkout, payment-handler, and PSP adapter services.

  • Use mTLS, OAuth client credentials, API keys, or allowlists where permissionless signatures are insufficient.

  • Sign deployment manifests and infrastructure configuration.

Proof evidence:

  • Profile fetch log.

  • HSM/KMS key attestation.

  • Runtime attestation report.

  • Gateway digest verification record.

  • Signed deployment manifest.

  • Service configuration hash.

Limits: Attestation proves the measured environment, not that the code is bug-free.

Layer 5: Evaluation and Observability

UCP relevance: This layer covers signed messages, checkout logs, cart logs, payment logs, identity logs, order webhooks, telemetry, and audit bundles.

Primary threats:

  • Logs are deleted, reordered, or rewritten after a disputed transaction.

  • Signed webhook is accepted for the wrong order.

  • Payment authorization response is not preserved.

  • Checkout completion evidence is incomplete.

  • Agent omits unfavorable telemetry.

  • Evaluation results are cherry-picked.

Controls:

  • Sign logs for cart, checkout, payment, identity, and order events.

  • Anchor event streams with hash chains or Merkle trees.

  • Verify webhook signatures and signer-to-order ownership.

  • Archive signed checkout completion and payment authorization responses.

  • Commit to evaluation datasets before testing.

  • Use out-of-band telemetry for critical enforcement points.

Proof evidence:

  • Merkle root.

  • Signed event log.

  • Webhook signature verification record.

  • Order ownership verification record.

  • Signed payment and checkout response archive.

  • Evaluation commitment and result signature.

Limits: A compromised component can produce false but validly signed logs. Behavioral monitoring and independent telemetry remain necessary.

Layer 6: Security, Governance, and Compliance

UCP relevance: This layer covers protocol versioning, capability governance, schema governance, payment-handler governance, identity scopes, consent policy, and change management.

Primary threats:

  • Public profile advertises unsupported or pre-release draft version.

  • Capability downgrade changes security semantics.

  • Vendor extension uses misleading namespace or schema origin.

  • OAuth scopes are overbroad or not mapped to operations.

  • Buyer consent is not connected to actual data handling.

  • Payment-handler specification changes without approval.

  • Natural-language governance policy diverges from executable policy.

Controls:

  • Enforce date-based UCP versions in public profiles.

  • Validate supported_versions profiles as complete leaf profiles.

  • Sign profile, schema, extension, and payment-handler changes.

  • Bind policy-as-code to UCP capability, scope, and state definitions.

  • Validate OAuth iss, PKCE S256, exact redirect_uri, revocation, and scope challenges.

  • Maintain multi-signature approval for material UCP changes.

  • Generate cross-layer audit bundles.

Proof evidence:

  • Signed governance manifest.

  • Signed change approval chain.

  • Formal policy verification result.

  • OAuth scope-to-operation mapping.

  • Consent enforcement evidence.

  • Cross-layer compliance bundle.

Limits: Proof shows that approved policy was enforced. It does not prove the policy was complete, ethical, or commercially wise.

Layer 7: Agent Ecosystem Security

UCP relevance: This layer covers platforms, businesses, credential providers, PSPs, agents, marketplaces, payment handlers, AP2 mandate issuers, and third-party extensions.

Primary threats:

  • Agent impersonates a trusted platform profile.

  • Business profile is fake, stale, or malicious.

  • Payment handler is unsupported, malicious, or misconfigured.

  • Payment credential is replayed against another checkout or business.

  • AP2 mandate is missing, expired, invalid, or bound to a different checkout.

  • Delegated authority chain exceeds user or organizational authorization.

  • Third-party plugin or extension compromises commerce flow.

Controls:

  • Verify UCP-Agent, message signature, signing key, and profile consistency.

  • Use profile trust tiers for high-risk merchants and platforms.

  • Require payment-handler provenance, schema validation, binding, and expiry.

  • Require AP2 mandates for autonomous or high-value completion.

  • Verify ap2.merchant_authorization, ap2.checkout_mandate, and payment mandate correlation.

  • Use threshold signatures for corporate procurement or regulated purchases.

  • Vet third-party agents, plugins, and extensions with supply-chain attestations.

Proof evidence:

  • Agent profile verification record.

  • Payment-handler attestation.

  • Payment credential binding proof.

  • AP2 mandate verification record.

  • Delegation-chain signature.

  • Third-party component provenance.

Limits: Identity and delegation proof do not prevent an authorized agent from making a poor decision within its permitted scope.

Section 8: Institutional Assurance Profile

The following requirements define a high-assurance UCP deployment profile.

POC-UCP-01: Profile Evidence

Each UCP commerce session must record:

  • business profile URL and hash;

  • platform profile URL and hash;

  • selected ucp.version;

  • selected supported_versions profile, if applicable;

  • signing key kid values used for verification;

  • profile fetch time and validation result.

POC-UCP-02: Negotiation Transcript

Each UCP commerce session must create a signed negotiation transcript containing:

  • selected service;

  • selected transport;

  • active capabilities and versions;

  • active extensions and versions;

  • schema URLs and schema hashes;

  • payment-handler IDs and versions;

  • identity-linking scopes relevant to the operation.

POC-UCP-03: Mandatory Signatures for State Changes

All state-changing UCP operations must be signed. This includes create, update, complete, cancel, identity, payment, order-management, and post-purchase actions.

POC-UCP-04: Material Response Signatures

Material responses must be signed and archived. At minimum:

  • checkout completion;

  • payment authorization;

  • payment failure;

  • identity authorization challenge;

  • order created;

  • order updated;

  • order canceled;

  • return or refund status.

POC-UCP-05: Checkout State Enforcement

Checkout state must be enforced outside the LLM:

  • requires_escalation must hand off through continue_url.

  • ready_for_complete is required for programmatic completion.

  • completed must be immutable.

  • AP2 or trusted deterministic UI is required for final buyer authorization.

POC-UCP-06: AP2 for Autonomous Completion

If no human is present in a trusted deterministic UI at completion time, the session must use dev.ucp.shopping.ap2_mandate or an equivalent non-repudiable authorization mechanism.

POC-UCP-07: Payment Binding

Payment credentials must be bound to:

  • business identity;

  • checkout ID;

  • payment handler;

  • amount;

  • currency;

  • expiry;

  • idempotency key;

  • mandate or user authorization, where applicable.

POC-UCP-08: Explicit Payment Instrument Constraints

Institutional payment-handler declarations should publish explicit availableinstruments. Absence of availableinstruments should be treated as too broad for high-risk payment flows unless justified by policy. Multiple instruments must be rejected unless dev.ucp.shopping.split_payments is negotiated; permitted combinations, allocation priority, idempotency, per-instrument results, and compensating reversals must be captured in the evidence bundle.

POC-UCP-09: Identity Scope Mapping

Every user-authenticated operation must map to a UCP scope or documented access policy. The mapping must be signed, versioned, and auditable.

POC-UCP-10: Signal Provenance

Signals used for risk, fraud, authorization, or rate limiting must be:

  • platform-observed or independently attested;

  • namespaced by reverse-domain name;

  • minimized to transaction need;

  • retained only according to policy;

  • linked to verification evidence when third-party asserted.

POC-UCP-11: Consent Enforcement

Buyer consent fields must be mapped to enforceable data-use policy. A consent record alone is insufficient; the system must prove downstream enforcement.

POC-UCP-12: Tamper-Evident Event Streams

Cart, checkout, payment, identity, and order events must be signed and anchored in append-only logs using hash chains or Merkle trees.

POC-UCP-13: Runtime Attestation for High-Risk Flows

High-risk flows should require runtime attestation for:

  • autonomous agent runtime;

  • merchant checkout service;

  • payment-handler service;

  • PSP adapter;

  • evidence-generation service.

POC-UCP-14: Supply-Chain Attestation

Agents, extensions, payment handlers, schema tooling, and plugin components should carry SBOM/SLSA-style provenance and signed approval records.

POC-UCP-15: Audit Bundle Generation

For each disputed, audited, or high-value transaction, the system should be able to produce a proof bundle containing:

  • profiles;

  • negotiation transcript;

  • signed requests and responses;

  • checkout state log;

  • AP2 mandate or UI review evidence;

  • payment binding proof;

  • identity scope proof;

  • signal and consent evidence;

  • signed order event stream;

  • runtime and supply-chain attestations, where applicable.

  • Bind payment credentials to checkout, merchant, handler, amount, currency, expiry, and mandate.

  • Require AP2 for autonomous or high-value completion.

  • Add runtime attestation for agent, checkout, payment-handler, and PSP services.

  • Connect buyer consent to policy-as-code enforcement.

  • Add supply-chain attestations for agents, payment handlers, plugins, and extensions.

Phase 3: Ecosystem Verification

Target: make proof portable across merchants, platforms, PSPs, auditors, and regulators.

  • Establish profile and key transparency.

  • Standardize proof bundle format.

  • Add privacy-preserving proofs for eligibility, loyalty, consent, and regulated compliance.

  • Use threshold signatures for corporate procurement and regulated purchases.

  • Integrate proof coverage, attestation freshness, and mandate verification into board and regulator reporting.

Figure 6 turns the roadmap into an assurance progression. Conformance comes first, then cryptographic evidence, cross-layer control assurance, and finally proof that can travel across merchants, platforms, payment providers, auditors, and regulators.

Figure 6: Proof-of-Control Adoption Roadmap

Section 11: Success Metrics

Table 8 converts the assurance framework into measurable operating targets. Most integrity controls require complete coverage because partial signing or transcript retention creates predictable blind spots; the two operational targets, sub-60-second proof-bundle generation and reduced manual evidence collection, test whether stronger assurance remains usable at institutional scale.

Table 8: Proof-of-Control Success Metrics

Section 12: Explicit Limitations

Proof-of-Control does not prove everything.

Digital signatures prove origin and integrity of a signed artifact. They do not prove business correctness.

Content-Digest proves raw body integrity for a transmitted HTTP body. It does not create durable semantic evidence unless the body and verification result are retained.

JWK key discovery proves which key was advertised in the profile's canonical keys[] JWK Set at fetch time. It does not prove profile history unless profile versions are retained or anchored.

OAuth identity linking proves scoped authorization according to token and scope policy. It does not prove the user understood every downstream agentic action.

AP2 mandates prove non-repudiable authorization for specified terms. They do not prove the agent selected the best product.

Runtime attestation proves measured code ran in a measured environment. It does not prove the code is free of bugs.

Formal verification proves properties against a formal specification. It does not prove that the specification captures all relevant business, legal, or ethical risks.

Tamper-evident logs reveal alteration or deletion. They do not guarantee that every real-world event was logged unless independent coverage controls exist.

Fairness, societal impact, recommendation quality, and consumer transparency require evaluation, policy, disclosure, and human governance in addition to cryptographic proof.

Section 13: Research and Maturity Roadmap

Table 9 distinguishes deployable next steps from problems that remain genuinely open. The near-term strategy is to bound high-risk workflows, prove narrow claims, and connect existing evidence sources; full verification of open-ended planning and manipulation-resistant reputation still require research rather than confident product promises.

Table 9: Research and Maturity Roadmap

Section 14: Conclusion

UCP supplies the protocol vocabulary for agentic commerce. Proof-of-Control supplies the evidence model required for institutional trust.

The question is not whether a platform says an agent acted correctly. The question is whether a verifier can independently reconstruct and validate the authority chain:

  • which business profile was active;

  • which platform profile was active;

  • which capabilities and extensions were negotiated;

  • which schemas and payment handlers were used;

  • which identity scopes or mandates authorized the action;

  • which checkout state allowed or blocked programmatic completion;

  • which payment credential was submitted and how it was bound;

  • which order events followed; and

  • whether the evidence is tamper-evident across parties.

Agentic commerce will not scale on contractual assurance alone. It needs protocol-level interoperability plus independently verifiable control evidence.

UCP provides many of the right primitives. Proof-of-Control makes those primitives mandatory, observable, retained, and defensible across the MAESTRO stack.

item.title: Demystifying Kimi K3: The Three Algorithms Behind the #1 Frontend Coding Model
item.description: On July 16, 2026, Moonshot AI released Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with a 1-million-token context window.
item.dc:creator: Ken Huang
item.content:encoded:
On July 16, 2026, Moonshot AI released Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with a 1-million-token context window. It is the largest open-weight model ever shipped. Within hours it landed at #4 overall on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and, more strikingly, debuted at #1 on LMArena's Frontend Code Arena, beating Claude Fable 5 on the benchmark that most directly measures production coding value.

I want to be precise about what is and is not remarkable here. K3 is not the single best model in the world. Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol still edge it on pure reasoning. What changed is the shape of the frontier. For eighteen months the story was that Chinese labs trailed by six to twelve months and that chip sanctions guaranteed the gap. K3 refutes both halves of that sentence at once. It arrives at the frontier immediately, and it does so as an open model that anyone can download on July 27.

This post is in two halves. The free half is the technical teardown: the three architectural innovations that make K3 work, and a forensic look at every benchmark where it ranks number one, including what each benchmark actually tests and why a first-place finish there means something. The paid half is the part you act on: the geopolitics of a state-adjacent frontier lab, the open-source strategy that K3's specific capabilities unlock, a practical FAQ for deploying it, questions worth sitting with, and my honest read on where this goes.

Three scaling problems, solved at once

Every large model fights three separate battles. Sequence length wants to blow up attention cost quadratically. Depth wants to dilute the signal from early layers as the stack grows. Width, in a Mixture-of-Experts model, wants to descend into routing chaos as you add experts. Most labs win one or two of these fights. Moonshot's claim, and the benchmarks broadly support it, is that K3 wins all three, for a combined 2.5 times better scaling efficiency than the K2 series.

The diagram above is the whole model in one frame. The sequence dimension is handled by Kimi Delta Attention. The depth dimension is handled by Attention Residuals. The width dimension is handled by Stable LatentMoE. They are independent innovations that compose, and the ellipse at the bottom is what you get when they stack: a 2.8-trillion-parameter model that only activates 50 to 60 billion parameters for any given token. That sparsity is the reason a model this large is economical to serve at all.

Kimi Delta Attention: giving every channel its own memory

Standard Transformer attention costs you quadratically in sequence length. At one million tokens, that is a wall. Linear-attention schemes like Mamba get around it, but historically at a real cost to expressiveness. Kimi Delta Attention, which Moonshot introduced in the Kimi Linear paper in October 2025 and scaled up dramatically for K3, takes a subtler route: it refines Gated DeltaNet by changing one thing about how the recurrent state forgets.

The picture holds the entire idea. On the left, standard DeltaNet multiplies the previous state by a single scalar decay factor. Every hidden dimension forgets at the same rate, which is a blunt instrument. On the right, KDA replaces that scalar with a vector, turned into a diagonal matrix, so each dimension in the recurrent state gets its own independent forgetting rate. In notation, the update goes from multiplying the prior state by a scalar to multiplying it by Diag of a vector. That is a small change on paper and a large one in practice: a channel holding a critical long-range fact can hold it, while a channel tracking something local can flush and reuse itself.

Moonshot built this on a specialized Diagonal-Plus-Low-Rank transition matrix and open-sourced the FlashKDA kernels, which hit a 1.72 to 2.22 times prefill speedup on H20 GPUs. The measured payoff from the Kimi Linear prototype is the headline: up to 6.3 times faster decoding at 1M context, up to a 75 percent reduction in KV cache, and quality that matched or beat full Multi-Head Latent Attention under fair comparison. This is the machinery that makes a 1M context window affordable rather than theoretical.

Attention Residuals: letting layers choose what to remember

Depth has a quieter failure mode. The standard residual connection adds each layer's output to a running sum, which means that as the stack grows past a hundred layers, hidden states balloon, gradients spread unevenly, and the contribution of early layers gets diluted into noise. Moonshot's Attention Residuals work, published March 2026, treats this as a retrieval problem instead of an accumulation problem.

On the left of this figure, information marches up the stack with a fixed skip connection at every step, no discrimination about what matters. On the right, each layer acts like a query that attends back over all earlier layers, pulling in exactly the representations it needs with learned weights. The arrows carry different alpha values because Layer 3 might want sixty percent of Layer 1 and only ten percent of Layer 0. The full version costs too much memory at scale, so K3 uses Block AttnRes: ordinary residuals inside a block, attention over depth only between blocks, which drops the cost from order Ld to order Nd. On the 48B Kimi Linear model this bought a 7.5-point jump on GPQA-Diamond and matched a baseline trained with 1.25 times more compute. This is how K3 actually benefits from its enormous depth instead of drowning in it.

Stable LatentMoE: 896 experts, 16 awake

Width is the flashiest number and the easiest to get wrong. K3 has 896 experts and activates just 16 of them per token, a sparsity of about 98.2 percent. The hard part of extreme sparsity is not the arithmetic, it is keeping routing stable and making sure experts are actually used rather than a handful hogging every token.

The routing diagram shows Moonshot's answer. Instead of the brittle heuristic load-balancing losses that plague many MoE models, K3 uses Quantile Balancing: a token routes to an expert if its router score lands in the top quantile, which is deterministic, hyperparameter-free, and guarantees even utilization with zero dead experts. Two supporting tricks matter. Per-Head Muon applies the Muon optimizer independently to each attention head for training stability, and the Sigmoid Tanh Unit activation is chosen specifically to avoid the dead-neuron pathology that rarely-activated experts are prone to. The result, the two green boxes in the figure, is roughly 50 to 60 billion active parameters per token out of 2.8 trillion total.

One more piece makes serving possible: quantization-aware training. K3 trains with MXFP4 weights and MXFP8 activations from the supervised fine-tuning stage onward, so the model learns to be resilient to the low-precision format it will be served in, rather than eating the usual 10 to 15 percent quality hit from quantizing a giant model after the fact.

Where K3 finishes first, and what that actually measures

The #4 overall ranking is the headline that traveled. The more interesting story is the handful of benchmarks where K3 finishes first outright, because those are the ones tied to real engineering value rather than composite trivia.

This summary board is the map for the rest of this section. Frontend Code Arena is the clean number-one. Program Bench and SWE-Marathon are the deep-engineering wins. The overall ratings underneath, a 57 on the Intelligence Index and a 76.24 on the Coding Index, place K3 fourth in the world overall and first among open models on web engineering. Now the detail on each.

Frontend Code Arena, and why a 17-place jump matters

Frontend Code Arena is a live human-preference benchmark on LMArena where models generate real HTML, CSS, and JavaScript from a prompt and humans vote on head-to-head pairs. What makes it hard, and meaningful, is that a frontend answer cannot be graded by "does it compile." A model can emit syntactically perfect HTML that renders with a broken layout, wrong colors, or buttons that do nothing. Serious frontend evaluation harnesses like FrontendBench run the generated code in a sandboxed Node.js plus Puppeteer plus Jest environment to check element presence, functional correctness, and interactive logic all three. The arena captures the same three axes through human judgment at scale.

The breakdown figure is the substance of the win. K3 took first place in six of seven frontend domains, e-commerce, dashboards, forms, landing pages, and web apps among them, losing only the gaming category to Fable 5. It debuted at 1679 Elo across 1,757 votes, a 17-place leap from Kimi K2.6, which sat at number eighteen, and its raw accuracy climbed from 33 to 46 percent generation over generation. The significance is not the Elo number itself, which still carries a plus or minus 17-point confidence band this early. It is that this is the first time an open-weight model has ranked ahead of every proprietary model on a comprehensive web-engineering board. Frontend is the most visible surface of AI-assisted development, the thing a user sees first, and an open model just took the top of it.

Program Bench: rebuild the program from the binary

Program Bench is a different and arguably harder animal. The agent is handed a compiled binary and its documentation and asked to reconstruct the complete source codebase that reproduces the program's behavior. This is not "write a function that passes a unit test." It forces interface discovery, architecture-level reasoning, and behavioral fidelity across more than one code path. A model can pass HumanEval by emitting one short correct function; Program Bench refuses to be gamed that way because the target is an entire working program, verified across multiple paths.

K3 is a top performer here, and the reasons line up exactly with its architecture. Reconstructing a whole codebase demands holding the entire thing in context, which the 1M window and KDA make affordable. Synthesizing a coherent architecture across many layers is precisely what Attention Residuals were built to help with. And the fifty-plus billion active parameters give it far more headroom than routine code completion needs, leaving capacity for the reasoning. This benchmark matters because it mirrors the real work of refactoring legacy systems, migrating codebases, and reverse-engineering software nobody has documentation for.

SWE-Marathon: can it work for days without cheating

SWE-Marathon is the closest thing we have to measuring a real engineering job. Tasks are ultra-long-horizon, building a compiler, optimizing a kernel, standing up a production service, the kind of work measured in hours to days rather than minutes. The numbers around it are staggering: mean rollout usage is 27.2 million tokens per task, with a right tail reaching 877 million, and individual long-horizon trials can cost hundreds of dollars to evaluate. A full sweep runs into the tens of thousands.

The subtle challenge SWE-Marathon exposes is benchmark integrity. Over a long enough horizon, agents start reward hacking, exploiting the scoring system instead of genuinely solving the task, which is why the benchmark ships full agent trajectories for scrutiny. K3 lands in the top three here. Its 1M context lets it hold entire project state without forgetting what it did an hour ago, and KDA's decoding speed is what makes rollouts this long computationally survivable in the first place. If Frontend Code Arena proves K3 can produce polished output, SWE-Marathon proves it can sustain the grind, and the grind is where most real software gets built.

The paid section below picks up from here: the geopolitics of a frontier model funded partly by a Chinese state-owned enterprise, the specific open-source strategy K3's capabilities make possible, a deployment FAQ with real cost math, questions I think are worth sitting with, and where I believe this goes next. The free analysis above stands on its own; the paid half is the part you can act on.

OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10

About this Series

Agentic skills are becoming first-class citizens of AI workflows.

They let AI systems call tools, retrieve data, modify files, trigger actions, use external services, and complete tasks across platforms. That power is useful, but it also changes the risk model. A skill is no longer just content. It can become an execution path.

The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 was created to help developers, security teams, platform operators, and AI builders understand where these risks show up and how to reduce them before they become production incidents.

This video series walks through all 10 risks in a practical way. Each episode explains the issue, gives examples, and points toward the controls teams should consider when building or reviewing agentic skill ecosystems.

AST02: Supply Chain Compromise

AST06: Weak Isolation

AST07: Update Drift

Watch them together on my Agentic AI YouTube Channel here

Who Should Watch

This series is for builders and defenders working with AI agents, skills, plugins, tool integrations, MCP-style connectors, automation workflows, and AI platform governance.

If you are building skills, review the risks before publishing.

If you are adopting third-party skills, use the Top 10 as a checklist before trusting them.

If you operate an AI platform, treat skill governance as part of your security architecture, not as an afterthought.

Thank You

Thank you to everyone who has supported the OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 project and the broader OWASP community work around agentic AI security.

Agentic systems are moving fast. Security guidance needs to move with them.

item.description: By Distributedapps.ai
item.dc:creator: Ken Huang
item.content:encoded:
Over the past 10 Substack posts, we have been writing about Claude Fable 5 from the ground up: prompts, loops, memory, tool use, harness control, and the security work needed to make agent systems fit for production.

While those posts were going out, our AI researchers at DistributedApps.ai were doing the parallel work behind the scenes. We took the public series, expanded it, added Mythos 5, and turned it into a book for engineers, security teams, and leaders who need more than a clever prompt.

Today we are pleased to publish Engineering Agentic AI with Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5.

The Kindle edition is now live on Amazon: Engineering Agentic AI with Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5. If you want the store version, that is the public purchase page. Paid subscribers should use the paid section below instead, because the book download is included there during this launch window.

Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 changed the shape of agent engineering for teams that care about security, cost, memory, tools, and repeatable behavior. The model matters, but the harness matters more. A team can have a strong model and still ship a brittle agent if it has no refusal path, no memory boundary, no tool policy, no fallback plan, and no telemetry that a security leader can trust.

The free part of this post explains why the book exists, who should read it, and where to buy the public Kindle edition. The paid section includes the book download, a chapter-by-chapter reading guide, and the launch offer for annual subscribers: 50% off, a $100 saving, limited to the next 50 subscribers for 5 days.

The problem we kept seeing

Most AI agent advice still starts in the prompt box.

That is useful, up to a point. A good prompt can raise the floor. It can shape style, ask for evidence, force a model to slow down, or define a role. But the teams building real agents run into a harder set of questions.

What should the agent remember?

When should it refuse?

Which tool call should require a boundary check?

How do you know a fallback path worked?

What should a reviewer see before the agent touches a customer workflow, a codebase, a security control, or a paid system?

Those questions do not live inside one prompt. They live in the harness around the model.

That is the core argument of our book titled Engineering Agentic AI with Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5. The next useful layer of agent work is not another list of magic words. It is the engineering discipline around prompts, loops, memory, tools, policy, observability, and launch review.

Why Fable 5 and Mythos 5 deserve a book

Fable 5 is useful because it pushes teams past single-turn prompting. It rewards better loop design, cleaner context boundaries, stronger memory practices, and careful tool use. Mythos 5 makes the security and governance side harder to ignore. It asks a different question: what happens when the model can reason, remember, act, and adapt inside a system that has real permissions?

The book treats those models as part of a working production stack.

That means prompts appear in the book, but they do not own the book. A prompt is one control. It sits beside memory gates, refusal criteria, tool scopes, canary checks, fallback routing, logs, review queues, and business metrics.

That framing matters because most agent failures do not look dramatic at first. They look like small misses:

  • A memory store keeps the wrong detail.

  • A tool call runs with too much authority.

  • A fallback path masks a policy failure.

  • A benchmark passes while the live workflow drifts.

  • A team cannot explain why the agent made one decision instead of another.

The book gives names and patterns to those failures. More important, it gives teams ways to design around them.

Who should read it

We recommend this book to three groups.

First, AI engineers who already know how to prompt and now need to build agents that survive contact with users, tools, and changing context. The book gives you a vocabulary for loops, memory, evals, and harness design.

Second, security architects and AppSec teams who need to review agent systems without pretending the model is a normal web app. The book turns prompt injection, memory poisoning, tool abuse, fallback risk, and observability gaps into reviewable engineering surfaces.

Third, engineering leaders who need a launch checklist that does not collapse into vibes. If you approve agent deployments, you need to know what evidence to ask for. The book helps you ask sharper questions before a team ships.

It is also useful for founders building AI products. A founder does not need a giant AI governance program on day one, but a founder does need the habit of treating agent behavior as something to design, test, and monitor.

The book's strongest idea

The strongest idea in the book is simple: agent capability without harness control is not a product strategy.

It is a liability with a nice demo.

That line sounds harsh, but we mean it in a practical way. If an agent can use tools, read context, write memory, summarize records, call APIs, or change state, then the harness becomes part of the product. Users feel the harness when it refuses the right request. Security teams feel it when tool scopes hold. Operators feel it when telemetry explains a failure before customers do.

The book keeps returning to that point. A strong agent system needs:

  • prompts that define behavior without pretending to be policy

  • loops that know when to continue, stop, or ask for review

  • memory that earns its right to persist

  • tools with narrow permissions and clear evidence

  • fallback paths that reveal risk instead of hiding it

  • telemetry that supports both debugging and governance

That is the shift from model enthusiasm to production engineering.

What makes the book useful

The book has 18 chapters. The first 10 grew out of the public article series. The next 8 move deeper into production concerns: launch review, economics, observability, security testing, governance, and operational practice.

That matters because most readers do not need one more high-level essay about agents. They need a path from "this demo works" to "this system can be reviewed, maintained, and improved."

The chapters are built for that path. You can read them straight through, but you can also use them as a field guide. If your current pain is memory, start there. If your current pain is prompt injection or tool safety, start with the harness and security chapters. If your current pain is leadership review, jump to the production chapters and work backward.

The book is strongest when you bring your own project to it. Read a chapter, then ask: where does our system do this today? Where are we guessing? Where would we be embarrassed if an auditor, customer, or incident reviewer asked for evidence?

That is where the book starts paying for itself.

Our recommendation

If you are building agentic AI systems this year, read this before your next launch review.

Do not read it as a manifesto. Read it as a checklist you can argue with. Mark the places where your current harness has a control. Mark the places where the team relies on hope. Then pick one chapter and turn it into an improvement ticket.

The book will help you avoid two common mistakes.

The first mistake is treating a better model as a substitute for engineering. Better models reduce some friction, but they also make it easier to build agents with broader reach. Reach needs controls.

The second mistake is treating security as a final review. Agent security belongs inside the loop design, the memory design, the tool design, and the monitoring design. If you wait until the end, you only get to say no. If you start early, you can design a safer yes.

That is the spirit of the book.

Why paid readers get the proof PDF

Paid subscribers are helping us do the harder work: turn public writing into practical field material for engineers, security teams, and leaders. That means drafts, proof copies, checklists, diagrams, and early versions of book material before it reaches a wider store channel.
